# Introduction

Forecasting tools can make it easy to generate predictions, but understanding how they work helps us decide when to rely on them. Different workloads have different patterns, and a model that works well for one may be less useful for another. In this post, I'll explore two forecasting approaches in R and test how well they predict phone volume.

Accurate phone forecasts can help teams balance phone coverage with other work and plan time for training, staff meetings, or system updates. My goal is to compare how well Prophet and ETS predict daily recorded inquiries for the next four weeks, focusing on Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. I'll use New York City's 311 inquiry data, starting with 2015–2017 for training and testing four-week forecasts against recorded activity in 2018. Each forecast will cover 20 weekdays, including holidays that fall on weekdays.

I'll start with Prophet, which models trends and recurring patterns and can incorporate holidays or other predictors. Then I'll explore ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonality), an exponential smoothing approach that gives more weight to recent observations. I'll compare their predictions against actual call volumes and finish with a recommendation for this dataset, including the limitations of that comparison.

# Set-up

Before building the forecasts, I'll load the packages and bring in the data we'll use throughout the analysis.

I'll use tidyverse and lubridate to prepare the data, Prophet and ETS to forecast volume, and a reusable `style_table()` function to format tables to match the blog.

```{r setup}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "lubridate", "httr2", "prophet", "forecast"))

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(prophet)
library(forecast)
source("data/R/style-table.R")
```

The [NYC 311 Call Center Inquiry dataset](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/311-Call-Center-Inquiry/wewp-mm3p/about_data) records agent-handled inquiries. I'll use saved hourly counts for 2015–2018, using the first three years for training and 2018 for testing. These counts exclude abandoned calls, and missing hours may not mean zero activity. This period also avoids pandemic-related underreporting beginning in March 2020.

```{r data}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false

data <- read_csv("data/nyc-311-data.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

```

# Explore the Data

The first six rows show the three fields we'll use: `date` identifies weekdays and separates our training and testing periods, `hour` lets us focus on 8 a.m.–5 p.m., and `inquiry_count` is the recorded volume we'll summarize and forecast. We'll focus on Monday–Friday. Because the counts reflect inquiries handled by agents, they may understate demand when callers hang up before reaching someone, which matters if we use the forecast to plan phone coverage.

```{r preview-data}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| fig-alt: "First six rows of the hourly inquiry data, showing date, hour, and inquiry count."

style_table(head(data))

```

## Historical Business-Hour Volume

I'll start by totaling inquiries for each weekday from 8 a.m. up to 5 p.m. and plotting the 2015–2017 training period. This gives us a first look at changes in volume, recurring patterns, and unusually high or low days before building either model. Days with missing business hours are left as gaps rather than treated as complete totals.

```{r historical-volume}
#| eval: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Line chart of daily recorded NYC 311 inquiries during weekday business hours, from 2015 through 2017. Days with missing hourly records are left as gaps."

daily <- expand_grid(
  date = seq(as.Date("2015-01-01"), as.Date("2017-12-31"), by = "day"),
  hour = 8:16
) |>
  filter(wday(date, week_start = 1) <= 5) |>
  left_join(data, by = c("date", "hour")) |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(
    inquiry_count = if (anyNA(inquiry_count)) NA_real_ else sum(inquiry_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(daily, aes(date, inquiry_count)) +
  geom_line(color = "#385E66", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily NYC 311 Inquiries",
    subtitle = "Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–5 p.m. | 2015–2017",
    x = NULL, y = "Recorded inquiries",
    caption = "Source: NYC Open Data. Days with missing business hours are not totaled."
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "serif", base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    text = element_text(color = "#283438"),
    plot.title = element_text(color = "#24434A", face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#DDDCD6"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#F5F3EF", color = NA),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#F5F3EF", color = NA),
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 9)
  )
```
